newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten vows to return to Hong Kong one day.
newsitem.headline: Patten vows to return to Hong Kong one day.

text.p: East and West bade farewell on Friday when British Governor Chris Patten stole a few hours from an overcrowded schedule to say goodbye to the ordinary men and women of Hong Kong -- and vowed to return one day.
With just four days before his job is done, the 28th and last British governor's final hours are filled with pomp, ceremony and back-to-back official functions.

He has a solemn investiture ceremony on Saturday when Prince Charles will bestow the last British knighthoods and other honours on Hong Kong's great and good. Sunday will be filled greeting visiting dignitaries before the last day of British rule on Monday June 30, crowned by the handover ceremony itself.

On Friday, his last chance to snatch a few hours away from formality, he rose early to host a morning phone-in show on government radio and spent the afternoon among the crowded tenements of the Kowloon peninsula shaking hands and sampling home-made snacks.
Patten has forecast June 30 will be a sad day for him.
"I hope I'll be able to return to Hong Kong one day," he told reporters a little wistfully.

The past five years have been turbulent ones for the British colony of 6.4 million people and for Patten, who nevertheless leaves a difficult job with his personal popularity riding high, an obvious fondness for the people of Hong Kong and its cuisine.

"I feel that I've eaten too much, that I haven't had quite enough sleep, and that I am looking forward to the day itself, to the ceremonies and to the beginning of a new chapter," he told radio listeners.
Patten infuriated China by ramming through mild electoral reforms, giving birth to Hong Kong's first elected legislature.
Chinese officials retaliated by reviling him as a serpent, a villain, and a "prostitute for a thousand generations", and will dismantle his reforms this July 1.
But opinion polls show, embarrassingly for Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, that he lags Patten, a light-haired "foreign devil" who does not speak Chinese.

Patten said he had found Chinese jibes easier to deal with than party political posturing in Britain. He quoted Confucius, who once said: "A gentleman, he is sent by his lord to serve in the four quarters of the globe and if he doesn't bring disgrace on his lord, that is a gentleman".

Tung, who also likes to quote the great philosopher, has yet to show he shares Patten's common touch, demonstrated from the very beginning when he arrived in 1992 wearing a lounge suit instead of the traditional feathers, pith helmet and sword.

He immediately embarked on a meet-the-people campaign to the amazement of a population used to the remote and lofty style of previous colonial governors and the secretive, withdrawn Chinese officials stationed at China's mission in Hong Kong.
Patten spent his last walkabout at the site of his first contacts with the Hong Kong public -- on the streets, estates and temples of the overcrowded Kowloon peninsula.

In one of the maze of courtyards of the Wong Tai Sing temple where thousands gather daily to pray for good fortune, he bowed to Chinese gods and set 108 songbirds free into the incense-laden air to the delight of hundreds of mainly elderly worshippers who crowded him seeking to touch his hand.
"Fei Pang, Pangyau" (Fatty Patten, Friend), said Mrs Ng, one of dozens of elderly women who queued for hours in the humidity of a summer afternoon for a glimpse of the last governor.

Ah Ying, aged 12, and his friends from a nearby public housing estate battled their way through the crowds to snap photographs. "Bye Bye, goodbye," they shouted waving furiously in an attempt to catch his eye. "Patten? He's number one."
